common_name: Stoke Red Apple (English Bittersharp Cider Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Stoke Red crops reliably once established and tolerates the damp West Country climate it was bred for.

directions: Originating in Somerset, England, Stoke Red is a small red-skinned cider apple classed as a bittersharp, carrying both significant tannin and bracing acidity that make it useful either as a blending component or, in larger proportion, as a backbone for a well-structured single-variety cider. It has long been grown in traditional Somerset orchards alongside better-known neighbors like Dabinett and Yarlington Mill, and it remains available through specialty cider-apple nurseries in England. Harvest in mid-to-late autumn once fruit drops freely, and press promptly, since the fruit is too astringent for fresh eating.
sources: Long Ashton Research Station cider apple classification

common_name: Tremlett's Bitter Apple (Devon Bittersweet Cider Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Tremlett's Bitter is vigorous and benefits from a somewhat larger allotted space than many other cider varieties.

directions: Originating in Devon, England, Tremlett's Bitter is one of the classic high-tannin bittersweet cider apples, grouped by the historic Long Ashton Research Station classification among the more astringent bittersweets used in traditional West Country cider blending. Its fruit contributes deep color and firm tannin structure to a blend and is still planted commercially in Devon and Somerset cider orchards as well as by American craft cideries sourcing heirloom English varieties. Harvest in mid-autumn and press soon after milling, since the small, hard, bitter fruit has no value for fresh eating.
sources: Long Ashton Research Station cider apple classification

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Ashton Bitter is a reasonably vigorous, reliable cropper suited to standard or half-standard orchard training.

directions: Selected and promoted from Somerset hedgerow stock by the Long Ashton Research Station, for which it is named, Ashton Bitter is a bittersweet variety chosen for its consistent tannin content and has become a standard component of English commercial cider blends. It is grown today both in West Country cider orchards and by smaller craft producers seeking a dependable bittersweet with good juice yield. Harvest in mid-autumn as fruit begins to drop, and mill promptly, since it is grown purely for cider.
sources: Long Ashton Research Station cider apple classification

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Chisel Jersey is vigorous, heavy-cropping, and well suited to modern bush or half-standard training systems.

directions: Part of the historic Somerset family of 'Jersey' cider apples that also includes Harry Masters Jersey, Chisel Jersey is a bittersweet variety prized by commercial cider makers for its combination of high, well-balanced tannin and reliable, heavy yields, and it remains one of the most widely planted bittersweet varieties in new English cider orchards today. Its fruit is small and dull green-russeted, far too astringent for fresh eating and intended purely for pressing. Harvest in mid-to-late autumn once fruit drops readily, and press soon after milling.

common_name: Browns Apple (Classic Somerset Bittersweet Cider Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Browns Apple is a strong, reliable grower that has long been favored for consistent annual cropping.

directions: Originating in Somerset, England, Browns Apple is one of the historic bittersweet varieties underpinning the traditional West Country cider industry, contributing dependable tannin and good juice volume to commercial blends produced by major Somerset cideries. Its fruit is medium-small, dull red-flushed, and borne in heavy clusters, making it an efficient variety for orchard harvest. Harvest in mid-autumn once fruit drops freely, and mill and press promptly, since it is grown exclusively for cider.
sources: Long Ashton Research Station cider apple classification

common_name: Sweet Coppin Apple (Devon Bittersweet Cider Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Sweet Coppin is a moderately vigorous, dependable cropper well suited to traditional Devon orchard spacing.

directions: Originating on a farm in Devon, England, Sweet Coppin is a bittersweet cider apple valued for its relatively high natural sugar content paired with soft tannin, letting it ferment to a good alcoholic strength without added sugar while still contributing body to a blend. It remains part of the traditional Devon and Somerset cider repertoire and is offered today by several specialty heritage fruit tree nurseries in the UK. Harvest in mid-to-late autumn as fruit drops, and press promptly, since it is grown for cider rather than fresh eating.

common_name: Tom Putt Apple (Dual-Purpose Culinary and Cider Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Tom Putt is a vigorous, hardy tree that crops heavily and tolerates exposed sites better than many finer cider varieties.

directions: A long-cultivated West Country heirloom associated with both Somerset and Devon, Tom Putt is a bright red, sharply acidic apple that has traditionally served a dual role, pressed for a sharp, refreshing single-variety or blending cider while also being used in the kitchen for cooking when picked slightly earlier. It is one of the more widely available old English apple varieties, still sold by numerous heritage and specialty fruit tree nurseries. Harvest from late summer into early autumn depending on intended use, picking earlier for cooking and later, once fruit drops, for pressing.

common_name: Slack ma Girdle Apple (Heirloom Somerset Cider Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Slack ma Girdle is a vigorous, spreading tree that benefits from generous spacing and periodic thinning.

directions: This whimsically named heirloom cider apple, traditionally associated with Somerset orchards, produces fruit so sweet and juice-heavy that, according to local folklore, overindulgence in the cider loosens one's belt, hence the name. It is a minor but genuine part of the historic West Country single-variety cider repertoire and continues to be propagated by a handful of specialty heritage and cider-apple nurseries in England. Harvest in mid-autumn once fruit drops readily, and press soon after milling, since it is grown for cider rather than fresh eating.

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; White Jersey is a moderately vigorous tree valued for steady, if not exceptionally heavy, cropping.

directions: Part of the historic group of Somerset 'Jersey' cider apples alongside Harry Masters Jersey and Chisel Jersey, White Jersey is a pale-skinned bittersweet variety that contributes mild, well-rounded tannin to traditional West Country cider blends. It has long been grown in Somerset orchards and continues to be available through UK nurseries specializing in heritage cider fruit trees. Harvest in mid-autumn once fruit drops freely, and mill and press promptly, since the fruit is intended purely for cider.
sources: Long Ashton Research Station cider apple classification

common_name: Binet Rouge Apple (Normandy Bittersweet Cider Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Binet Rouge is a vigorous, productive tree traditionally grown as a tall standard in the high orchards typical of Normandy cider country.

directions: One of the classic cider apples of Normandy, France, Binet Rouge is a red-skinned bittersweet variety that contributes good tannin and aromatic character to traditional Norman cidre and is also used in the production of Calvados brandy. It remains a staple variety in Norman orchards, and nurseries specializing in traditional French cider apples continue to propagate it. Harvest in mid-to-late autumn once fruit drops, and press promptly, since the fruit is grown for cider and distillation rather than fresh eating.
sources: Institut Français des Productions Cidricoles (IFPC) variety reference

common_name: Fréquin Rouge Apple (Normandy Bittersweet Cider Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Fréquin Rouge is traditionally trained as a tall standard tree in the open, grass-grazed orchards characteristic of Norman cider production.

directions: This red-skinned bittersweet apple is one of the most historically important cider varieties of Normandy, France, valued for its generous juice yield and the firm tannin structure it lends to traditional cidre blends. It remains widely planted in Norman cider orchards today and is offered by nurseries specializing in traditional French cider apple varieties. Harvest in mid-autumn once fruit drops freely, and press promptly, since it is grown for cider rather than fresh eating.
sources: Institut Français des Productions Cidricoles (IFPC) variety reference

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Guillevic is a vigorous, traditionally trained standard tree suited to the open orchards of Brittany.

directions: Originating in Brittany, France, Guillevic is a bitter cider apple that contributes significant tannin with relatively little acidity to traditional Breton cidre, where it is prized for structure in blends alongside sweeter varieties. It continues to be grown by traditional Breton cider producers and is propagated by nurseries specializing in regional French cider apple heritage varieties. Harvest in mid-autumn once fruit drops, and press promptly, since the fruit is intended purely for cider production.
sources: Institut Français des Productions Cidricoles (IFPC) variety reference
